summary: Describes an allocation plan for IPv6 addresses to be used while testing prototype IPv6 software. It was an experimental arrangement meant for early test networks and was replaced by RFC 2471.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 1897 describes temporary IPv6 addresses for testing prototype software. The addresses were not meant for general Internet routing, and users would eventually have to change them; RFC 2471 later replaced this plan.

questions: how were early ipv6 test networks addressed
how did early ipv6 testing work
how were ipv6 test addresses structured
subtitle: A temporary IPv6 address plan for testing prototype software.

tldr.problem: People testing IPv6 prototype software needed addresses reserved for testing rather than ordinary Internet use.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC assigns a provider-based IPv6 address format with a reserved registry ID and fields based partly on a provider's autonomous system number and an IPv4 network address.
tldr.outcome: These temporary addresses had to be replaced. RFC 2471 obsoletes this RFC.

facts.label: Interface ID
facts.value: Usually a 48-bit IEEE 802 MAC address, if available

sections.title: Temporary Addresses for IPv6 Testing
sections.content:
RFC 1897 describes an allocation plan for IPv6 addresses used to test prototype software. The addresses are temporary and will be reclaimed, so systems using them will have to renumber later.

The RFC says these addresses are not to be routable on the Internet except for IPv6 testing. They may be assigned manually, through IPv6 automatic address allocation, or through DHCP for IPv6.
sections.plainLanguage: These addresses let people test IPv6 software before using regular addresses. They were temporary, so systems using them would later need different addresses.

sections.title: Fields in a Test Address
sections.content:
The format follows provider-based unicast addressing. It starts with the format prefix 010 and the IANA-reserved registry ID 11111. Later fields carry the service provider's autonomous system number, part of the subscriber's IPv4 network address, a subnet address and an interface identifier.

The reserved fields must be set to zero. The subnet address identifies a physical link, while the interface identifier uniquely identifies an interface on that link; the RFC says this is usually the interface's 48-bit IEEE 802 MAC address when available.
sections.plainLanguage: The address has separate fields for the test allocation, the provider, the subscriber's network, a subnet and a network interface. This structure lets testers organize addresses for their own networks.

sections.title: Deriving Network and Subnet Values
sections.content:
The provider field uses the autonomous system number of the organization providing Internet service. The IPv4 network field takes the high-order 24 bits of the subscriber's current routable IPv4 address.

This method works directly when the subscriber's IPv4 prefix is no longer than 24 bits. For a longer prefix, the RFC says to use the remaining IPv4 prefix bits as the high-order bits of the subnet address. Subscribers choose subnet values; one suggested method is to use the bits that identify the IPv4 subnet.
sections.plainLanguage: Some address fields come from the organization's existing provider and IPv4 network information. The subscriber chooses subnet values, following the special handling described for longer IPv4 prefixes.

sections.title: Replacement and Security Note
sections.content:
The unit metadata says RFC 1897 is obsoleted by RFC 2471. RFC 1897 itself describes the allocation as temporary and says users will need to renumber.

The RFC's security considerations section says that security issues are not discussed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: RFC 1897's address plan was temporary and has been replaced by RFC 2471. The document does not discuss security issues.
